Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
SMA 1 (WMU 302,303, and 400) and SMA 2 (WMU 303, 306, 
308 and 402) Aerial Bighorn Sheep Survey (2018) 
 
Background 
Since 1971 in the Crowsnest District, aerial surveys for bighorn sheep have been conducted  to determine current 
population size estimates and herd composition, within known winter range. The most recent survey of Sheep 
Management Area (SMA) 1 and 2 took place in 2011, with only a partial survey being completed due to technical 
issues with aircraft and inclement weather. Since 1988, expansion of survey areas have occurred and only the 
Yarrow Creek – Castle unit has consistent data sets on sex-age ratios and abundance, to analyze long-term trends 
back to 1971. Due to the large-scale die-off of bighorn sheep in this unit due to a pneumonia outbreak in 1982, 
increased effort to survey this area has been recognized and is currently identified as a provincial priority for 
disease surveillance. Surveys were scheduled in 2015, 2016, and 2017 but unfortun ately, were not completed due 
to a combination of constraints including weather (lack of snow and high winds) and funding.  
More detailed information about sheep management, harvest, and licensing can be found at:  
 Bighorn Sheep Management  
 Hunting Draws Reports  
 
Survey Method 
Eight primary winter ranges were searched in detail, in addition to historically mapped snow free areas. The goal of 
the survey was to replicate past recent surveys of 2005 and 2011 for SMA 1 and 2 (Figure 1), to produce a 
minimum total trend count of Bighorn Sheep in accordance with provincial aerial ungulate survey protocols. 
Extensive review of historical aerial survey bighorn sheep sightings were also used, to ensure all known winter 
range habitat was identified and knowledge of wintering sheep distribu tion for the SMA’s were used for the survey. 
Flights were conducted on February 9th, 20th and 21st (6.2, 8.5 and 5.4 hours respectively), 2018 for a combined 
total of 20.1 hrs of survey effort to complete the survey. Aircraft used was a Bell 206 L3 Helicop ter (Ascent 
Helicopters Ltd.) with rear bubble windows. Depending on the day of the flight, a 3 -person Alberta Environment 
and Parks (AEP) based crew comprised the survey crew (Grant Chapman, Greg Hale, Mike Grue, Anne Loosen, 
Joel Nicholson and Maria Didkowsky). Pilot was Greg Goodison. Survey conditions were excellent – bright clear 
days, immediately after major snow events of >30 cm with cold temperatures (range minus 22 to 29 degrees 
Celsius), and minimal wind. Sheep were classified into age, sex, and horn curl categories as per Alberta 
Environment and Parks (AEP), Aerial Ungulate Survey Protocol (2009). Classification was further aided by high 
quality digital cameras and lenses (Nikon D3300 24 megapixel camera with 70 -300 mm image stabilized lens), 
aiding classification during and after survey flights. All bighorn sheep observed during survey were photographed 
and catalogued (758 images). Also, all other big game sightings were recorded.

Results  
Table 1 provides a summary of the 2018 aerial bighorn sheep survey for SMA’s 1 and 2. A total of 129 groups of 
bighorn sheep were detected comprising of 779 total individuals observed – with 768 (98.6%) being successfully 
classified. Due to the increased efficiency of the survey and previous expansion, near perfect survey conditions, 
and additional search effort, the 2018 minimum total count of 779 is the highest on record for SMA 1 and 2. This 
does not include recently completed Parks Canada’s 2018 aerial survey for bighorn sheep or historical survey 
effort within Wateron Lakes National Park (WLNP).

Please note – Comparison table and historical trend analysis unavailable at this time. Previous “winter range” 
survey data needs to be integrated with SMA boundaries, then sorted and checked for accuracy. Please check 
back for update. 
 
Total number of mature rams that are greater than 4/5 fifth’s horn curl appear to have declined compared to 
previous aerial surveys of 2005 and 2011 overall. Ewe to lamb ratio’s for SMA 1 and 2 of 35% and 33% 
respectively, are consistent with 2011 survey results and are within acceptable limits to maintain existing 
populations. Expanded analysis of historical data will provide additional insights regarding age, sex, herd 
composition and population trend in the near future.
